tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    19  Actions in Section 301 Investigations of Acts, Policies, and Practices 
    20  of Various Economies Related to the Failure To Impose and Effectively 
    21  Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced With Forced 
    22  Labor
    23  
    24  AGENCY: Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
    25  
    26  ACTION: Notice of determinations, request for comments, and notice of 
    27  public hearings.
    28  
    29  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    30  
    31  SUMMARY: On March 12, 2026, the United States Trade Representative 
    32  (Trade Representative) initiated 60 investigations related to the 
    33  failure of various economies to impose and effectively enforce a 
    34  prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor. The 
    35  Trade Representative has determined that 54 of the investigated 
    36  economies have failed to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor 
    37  import prohibition. The Trade Representative has determined that six of 
    38  the investigated economies have failed to effectively enforce a forced 
    39  labor import prohibition. The Trade Representative has determined that 
    40  the failure of each of the investigated economies to impose and 
    41  effectively enforce a force labor import prohibition is unreasonable 
    42  and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce. As a result of the findings in 
    43  each investigation, the Trade Representative proposes that appropriate 
    44  action includes additional duties on all products of the investigated 
    45  economies, except as provided in Annex A to this Notice. For economies 
    46  that impose a forced labor import prohibition; have taken on 
    47  commitments related to forced labor import prohibitions through an 
    48  Agreement on Reciprocal Trade; or have imposed a partial regime with 
    49  the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods, 
    50  the Trade Representative proposes 10% as the rate of additional duties. 
    51  For all other economies, the Trade Representative proposes 12.5% as the 
    52  rate of additional duties. The Trade Representative also proposes a 
    53  textile mechanism that would allow for a certain volume of apparel and 
    54  textile imports from certain economies to enter the United States at a 
    55  reduced Section 301 tariff rate. USTR seeks public comments on the 
    56  proposed actions in the investigations and will hold public hearings in 
    57  connection with the proposals.
    58

    61  appear at the hearings, along with a summary of the testimony, by this 
    62  date.

    65  hearings in the main hearing room of the U.S. International Trade 
    66  Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, beginning at 10:00 
    67  a.m., and continuing, as appropriate.
    68      Five days after the last day of the public hearings: Submit post-
    69  hearing rebuttal comments.

    82  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    83  
    84  I. Proceedings in the Investigations
    85  
    86      On March 12, 2026, the Trade Representative initiated 60 
    87  investigations related to the failure of various economies to impose 
    88  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
    89  produced wholly or in part with forced labor (forced labor import 
    90  prohibition), pursuant to section 302(b)(1) of the Trade Act of 1974, 
    91  as amended (Trade Act) (19 U.S.C. 2412(b)(1)). See 91 FR 12884 (March 
    92  17, 2026). The notice of initiation solicited written comments on, 
    93  inter alia: whether any economy subject to these investigations 
    94  maintains or is in the process of establishing a forced labor import 
    95  prohibition, and whether any such import prohibition is being 
    96  effectively enforced; the extent to which the failure of any economy to 
    97  establish and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is 
    98  unreasonable, discriminates against U.S. goods, or constitutes a 
    99  persistent pattern of conduct that permits any form of forced or 
   100  compulsory labor; the extent to which the failure of any economy to 
   101  establish and effectively enforce a
   102  
   103  [[Page 34273]]
   104  
   105  forced labor import prohibition has negatively affected U.S. commerce, 
   106  such as through lost U.S. exports or economic output, lower prices for 
   107  U.S. goods, or lower wages for U.S. workers; and what action, if any, 
   108  should be taken to address these issues.
   109      Interested persons filed over 450 written comments in response to 
   110  the notice, including post-hearing rebuttal comments. In addition, USTR 
   111  and the Section 301 Committee convened public hearings from April 28-
   112  29, 2026, during which nearly 60 witnesses provided testimony and 
   113  responded to questions. The public submissions are available at: 
   114  https://comments.ustr.gov/s/ at docket numbers USTR-2026-0133 and USTR-
   115  2026-0134. Transcripts of the hearings are available on USTR's website.
   116      On March 12, 2026, the date the investigations were initiated, the 
   117  Trade Representative requested consultations with the governments of

   172      Based on information obtained during the investigations, including 
   173  the confidential government-to-government consultations, the public 
   174  comments, testimony obtained at the public hearings, the confidential 
   175  advice of the appropriate advisory committees, and the Section 301 
   176  Committee, USTR prepared a comprehensive report, Acts, Policies, and 
   177  Practices of Various Economies Related to the Failure to Impose and 
   178  Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced 
   179  with Forced Labor (the ``Report''), regarding the acts, policies, and 
   180  practices of each economy under investigation. For each investigation,

   184  unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus

   187  website.

   189  II. The Acts, Policies, and Practices of the Investigated Economies 
   190  Related to the Failure To Impose and Effectively Enforce a Forced Labor 
   191  Import Prohibition
   192  
   193      Forced labor may be understood as work or service exacted from a 
   194  person under the menace of any penalty for its nonperformance and for 
   195  which the worker does not offer himself voluntarily. There is universal 
   196  international consensus that forced labor is a practice that should not 
   197  be tolerated. Numerous international instruments, such as the United 
   198  Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the International 
   199  Labour Organization (ILO) Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 
   200  (No. 105); the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 
   201  (1976); and the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at 
   202  Work and its Follow-up (1998), as amended in 2022, contain provisions 
   203  seeking to eliminate forced labor. Despite this clear and longstanding 
   204  consensus, the use of forced labor across the world continues to 
   205  persist and has even increased in recent years.
   206      The United States has long recognized that eliminating forced labor 
   207  is a moral and economic imperative and that trade is a critical means 
   208  to assist in that goal. For nearly 100 years, the United States has 
   209  prohibited the importation of goods produced with forced labor under 
   210  Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1307). Commitments to 
   211  prohibit forced labor imports in the United States--Mexico--Canada 
   212  Agreement, as well as in recently signed Agreements on Reciprocal 
   213  Trade, reflect the increasing awareness of this issue and recognition 
   214  that the adverse effects of trade in forced labor goods must be 
   215  addressed.
   216      The existence of forced labor imports in markets across the globe 
   217  has nurtured an economic system that permits the use of forced labor or 
   218  forced labor inputs, penalizing firms and economies that do not. By 
   219  prohibiting forced labor domestically and effectively enforcing its 
   220  forced labor import prohibition, the United States aims to ensure that 
   221  neither domestically produced products nor imports can gain a 
   222  competitive advantage in the U.S. market through the use of forced 
   223  labor. This helps ensure that competition in the U.S. market is based 
   224  on legitimate factors, such as quality and innovation, rather than an 
   225  artificial cost advantage from the illicit use of forced labor.
   226      Economies that fail to impose and effectively enforce a forced 
   227  labor import prohibition fail to ensure that market competition in 
   228  their jurisdiction occurs on a level basis with respect to labor costs. 
   229  While the vast majority of economies prohibit forced labor 
   230  domestically, such measures, if effectively enforced, only discipline 
   231  domestic producers. However, as demonstrated in the Report, these 
   232  measures fail to discipline the influx of imported forced labor goods 
   233  or to prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs.
   234  
   235  III. Determinations on Acts, Policies, and Practices Under 
   236  Investigation
   237  
   238      Based on the information obtained during the investigations, as 
   239  reflected in the Report, and considering the advice of the appropriate 
   240  advisory committees and Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative 
   241  has made the following determinations under sections 301(b) and 304(a) 
   242  of the Trade Act (19 U.S.C. 2411(b) and 2414(a)): the acts, policies, 
   243  and practices of each of the 60 economies covered in the investigations 
   244  are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and thus are 
   245  actionable under section 301(b) of the Trade Act.
   246  
   247  [[Page 34274]]
   248  
   249      In particular, the Trade Representative has determined:
   250       The following 54 economies have failed to impose and 
   251  effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced 
   252  with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; 
   253  Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People's Republic 
   254  of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; 
   255  Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; 
   256  Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New 
   257  Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; 
   258  Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri 
   259  Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; 
   260  T[uuml]rkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; 
   261  and Vietnam.
   262       The following six economies have failed to effectively 
   263  enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced 
   264  labor: Canada; Ecuador; the European Union; Indonesia; Mexico; and 
   265  Pakistan.
   266       Therefore, all of the investigated economies have failed 
   267  both to impose a forced labor import prohibition and to effectively 
   268  enforce such a prohibition.
   269       The failure of each of the investigated economies to 
   270  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is 
   271  unreasonable because it: (1) undermines the universal aim of 
   272  eliminating forced labor; (2) permits firms that avail themselves of 
   273  forced labor to produce goods at lower cost and thereby distort market 
   274  conditions for firms that do not use forced labor; (3) undermines the 
   275  profitability of firms that do not use forced labor; and (4) 
   276  contributes to the circumvention of existing forced labor import 
   277  prohibitions.
   278       The failure of each of the above-listed economies to 
   279  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition 
   280  burdens or restricts U.S. commerce by subjecting U.S. producers to 
   281  unfair competition from forced labor goods both in export markets and 
   282  the U.S. market, and by displacing foreign goods produced without 
   283  forced labor or forced labor inputs into the United States and other 
   284  markets.
   285  
   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,

   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of

   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.

   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import

   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import

    68  Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address 
    69                  Fundamental International Payments Problems
    70  
    71                  By the President of the United States of America
    72  
    73                  A Proclamation
    74  
    75                  1. The United States plays a pivotal role in shaping 
    76                  the global economy. At the same time, the United States 
    77                  faces various threats to its own economy and national 
    78                  interests. Sometimes, the United States faces 
    79                  fundamental international payments problems, such as 
    80                  large and serious balance-of-payments deficits, an 
    81                  imminent and significant depreciation of its currency 
    82                  in foreign exchange markets, or an international 
    83                  balance-of-payments disequilibrium. These problems can, 
    84                  among other things, endanger the ability of the United 
    85                  States to finance its spending, erode investor 
    86                  confidence in the economy, and distress the financial 
    87                  markets.
    88  
    89                  2. Special import measures to restrict imports, such as 
    90                  surcharges and quotas, are key tools to protect the 
    91                  economy and national security of the United States, 
    92                  and, in certain circumstances, they are required to 
    93                  deal with fundamental international payments problems.
    94  
    95                  3. Given the gravity of fundamental international 
    96                  payments problems and the importance of import 
    97                  restrictions as economic, national security, and 
    98                  foreign policy tools, Federal law, including section 
    99                  122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132) (section 
   100                  122), empowers the President to take action through 
   101                  surcharges and other special import restrictions to 
   102                  address fundamental international payments problems.
   103  
   104                  4. I have received certain requested information and 
   105                  opinions from senior officials on whether any 
   106                  fundamental international payments problems exist and 
   107                  the extent to which such problems could impair United 
   108                  States national interests, including economic and 
   109                  national security interests. The information and 
   110                  opinions discuss, among other things, the state of the 
   111                  balance of payments of the United States, the standing 
   112                  of the United States dollar in foreign exchange 
   113                  markets, and the state of international balances of 
   114                  payments. I have also received opinions and 
   115                  recommendations from senior officials on whether 
   116                  special import measures to restrict imports are 
   117                  required to address any fundamental international 
   118                  payments problems. These opinions address, among other 
   119                  things, whether a surcharge in the form of ad valorem 
   120                  duties is required to restrict imports to deal with 
   121                  large and serious United States balance-of-payments 
   122                  deficits, to prevent an imminent and significant 
   123                  depreciation of the United States dollar in foreign 
   124                  exchange markets, or to cooperate with other countries 
   125                  in correcting an international balance-of-payments 
   126                  disequilibrium.
   127  
   128                  5. These senior officials have informed me that 
   129                  fundamental international payments problems within the 
   130                  meaning of section 122 exist and that special import 
   131                  measures to restrict imports are required to address 
   132                  these problems. Specifically, my advisors have 
   133                  determined that an import surcharge in the form of ad 
   134                  valorem duties is required to deal with large and 
   135                  serious United States balance-of-payments deficits. My 
   136                  advisors have also opined that certain products should 
   137                  not be subject to the surcharge because of the needs of 
   138                  the United States economy and that the recommended 
   139                  exceptions are consistent with the limitations of 
   140                  section 122, the purposes of section 122, and the 
   141                  national interest of the United States.
   142  
   143  [[Page 9340]]
   144  
   145                  6. Among other things, I have been informed by my 
   146                  advisors that the United States balance-of-payments 
   147                  position, under any reasonable understanding of the 
   148                  term in the context of section 122, is currently a 
   149                  large and serious deficit. My advisors have studied 
   150                  different methods of evaluating balance-of-payments 
   151                  deficits, including calculations based on current-
   152                  account statistics. In my advisors' opinions, under any 
   153                  of these methods, the United States balance-of-payments 
   154                  position is a large and serious deficit.
   155  
   156                  7. For instance, my advisors have informed me that the 
   157                  United States runs a deficit in selling goods and 
   158                  services overseas, as reported by the United States 
   159                  Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the ``balance on 
   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently 
   167                  make a net income from the capital and labor that it 
   168                  deploys abroad, and experiences more transfer payments, 
   169                  on net, flowing out of the country than into the 
   170                  country.
   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy
   236  
   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.
   243  
   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    38                  Section 1. Purpose. The United States has imposed 
    39                  tariffs under various statutory authorities and through 
    40                  a number of Executive Orders and proclamations to 
    41                  protect national security and address unusual and 
    42                  extraordinary threats to the national security, foreign 
    43                  policy, and economy of the United States. Although each 
    44                  of these actions, as listed in section 2 of this order, 
    45                  serves separate and distinct policy purposes, I have 
    46                  now determined that, to the extent these tariffs apply 
    47                  to the same article, these tariffs should not all have 
    48                  a cumulative effect (or ``stack'' on top of one 
    49                  another) because the rate of duty resulting from such 
    50                  stacking exceeds what is necessary to achieve the 
    51                  intended policy goals. To avoid the cumulative effect 
    52                  of overlapping tariffs on certain articles, this order 
    53                  sets out the procedure for determining which of 
    54                  multiple tariffs shall apply to an article when that 
    55                  article is subject to more than one of the actions 
    56                  listed in section 2 of this order.

    80                  Southern Border), Executive Order 14227 of March 2, 
    81                  2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Situation at 
    82                  Our Southern Border), and Executive Order 14232 of 
    83                  March 6, 2025 (Amendment to Duties to Address the Flow

    85                      (d) Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595  
  1596  [[Page 47331]]
  1597  
  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and 
  1599  paprika products, lithium hexafluorophosphate, and forgings and 
  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain 
  1602  economies is linked to certain acts, policies, and practices found 
  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products 
  1604  would benefit foreign exporters of beef produced with forced labor at 
  1605  the expense of the American cattle producer. Similarly, commenters 
  1606  suggested that paprika and paprika derived products, lithium 
  1607  hexafluorophosphate, and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1608  pesticides are imported from certain economies linked to certain acts, 
  1609  policies, and practices found actionable in these investigations.
  1610      Additionally, commenters suggested that imports of these products 
  1611  are available from domestic sources and are putting pressure on 
  1612  domestic producers. With respect to paprika and paprika derived 
  1613  products, commenters suggested that imports have caused market 
  1614  disruptions, preventing U.S. production of these products. 
  1615  Additionally, comments reported that imports of lithium 
  1616  hexafluorophosphate and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1617  pesticides have inhibited U.S. production of these products. Commenters 
  1618  pointed to recent and anticipated expansion in U.S. production 
  1619  capabilities, and suggested that imposing tariffs on these products 
  1620  could support investment and employment in domestic production. With 
  1621  respect to forgings and articles containing forgings, commenters 
  1622  suggested that these products are readily available from domestic 
  1623  sources, at reasonable prices, in sufficient quantities and that 
  1624  subjecting imports of these products to tariffs could support 
  1625  investment and employment in the United States. Similarly, comments 
  1626  suggested that the domestic avocado industry is under significant 
  1627  pressure due to low-priced avocado imports and applying tariffs would 
  1628  benefit certain U.S. agricultural producers.
  1629      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1630  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1631  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1632  Representative has determined not to remove these products from the 
  1633  list of exempted products. There remains limited availability of these 
  1634  products from domestic sources, a point conceded by one commenter 
  1635  regarding paprika. Regarding claims that these products should be 
  1636  subject to the tariffs because they are related to acts, policies, and 
  1637  practices found actionable in these investigations, Section 
  1638  301(c)(3)(B) provides that the Trade Representative is authorized to 
  1639  take action against any goods or economic sector ``without regard to 
  1640  whether or not such goods or economic sector were involved in the act, 
  1641  policy, or practice that is the subject of such action.''
  1642  
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.
  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the 
  1664  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope 
  1666  of actions: certain animal products; certain seeds; certain vegetable 
  1667  products; certain sugar and sugar containing products; unflavored 
  1668  instant coffee; certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain 
  1669  animal hides and leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and 
  1670  hydroxides; pig iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain 
  1671  aluminum scrap waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious 
  1672  metals or precious metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; 
  1673  certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals 
  1674  and pharmaceutical ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and 
  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental 
  1690  and production conditions, such as additional growing seasons. 
  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as 
  1693  certain varieties of seed will no longer be viable for 
  1694  commercialization in the United States.
  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the 
  1698  proposed product exemptions are limited to products used for religious 
  1699  purposes only. According to comments, products in the relevant HTSUS 
  1700  subheading are essential growing-media and fiber inputs used in nursery 
  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute 
  1702  burlap, and sisal twine. According to comments, the crops used to 
  1703  produce these products are not commercially grown in the United States 
  1704  given climate limitations and, therefore, there is no domestic industry 
  1705  capable of producing these inputs for the U.S. horticulture sector.
  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are 
  1708  more efficient than ever and domestic sugar yields have increased, yet 
  1709  the United States has never produced enough sugar to meet its domestic 
  1710  demand. To meet this demand, the United States has historically had to 
  1711  import significant amounts of sugar. According to comments, U.S. sugar 
  1712  processing
  1713  
  1714  [[Page 47332]]
  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and 
  1717  supply a critical input of the U.S. food supply chain.
  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that 
  1719  unflavored instant coffee is not available from domestic sources in 
  1720  sufficient quantities for U.S. consumers and coffee companies, 
  1721  including value-added manufacturers. These comments also maintained 
  1722  that over 99 percent of instant coffee imports come from economies 
  1723  covered by these investigations and there are not adequate non-tariffed 
  1724  alternatives. Commenters also noted that U.S. coffee companies will 
  1725  continue to be at a disadvantage producing and innovating ready-to-
  1726  drink and cold brew coffee compared to their foreign competitors if 
  1727  tariffs on unflavored instant coffee are imposed.
  1728      With respect to certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs, 
  1729  commenters noted that imposing additional duties on these chemicals 
  1730  could cause disruptions or shortages in the domestic supply due to the 
  1731  limited availability of certain active ingredients outside of the 
  1732  investigated economies and because these products cannot be produced in 
  1733  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1734  Commenters also noted that the exemptions would be essential to avoid 
  1735  tariff inversion, causing U.S. manufacturers who produce value-added 
  1736  products to be disadvantaged in comparison to importers of finished 
  1737  agriculture chemical products.
  1738      With respect to certain animal hides and leather products, 
  1739  commenters noted that certain types of exotic leather--including 
  1740  reptile and ostrich--cannot be obtained in the United States because 
  1741  there is no domestic supply. According to commenters, tariffs would 
  1742  cause the migration of exotic leather manufacturing and American jobs 
  1743  to other countries, such as Mexico.
  1744      With respect to certain wood and wood products, commenters noted 
  1745  that certain types of wood and wood product imports--including 
  1746  eucalyptus and certain eucalyptus products--are not available from 
  1747  domestic producers in sufficient quantities to meet U.S. demand. 
  1748  According to commenters, these products are raw material inputs that 
  1749  are used to make timber and crane mats necessary in U.S. construction, 
  1750  powerline installation, and heavy civil infrastructure.
  1751      With respect to vanadium oxides and hydroxides, commenters noted 
  1752  that these products are necessary critical mineral inputs for which 
  1753  there is no or insufficient primary production in the United States and 
  1754  additional tariffs on these materials would cause serious supply 
  1755  dislocations for critical energy-storage infrastructure including AI 
  1756  data centers, electric-grid resiliency, and defense applications. 
  1757  According to comments, vanadium and vanadium electrolytes are necessary 
  1758  inputs across multiple sectors, including steel (including high-
  1759  strength, low-alloy steels for construction, pipelines, and automotive 
  1760  applications); titanium alloys used in aerospace and defense; and 
  1761  critical energy-storage.
  1762      With respect to pig iron, commenters noted that, historically, more 
  1763  than 95 percent of domestic pig iron production has been consumed 
  1764  internally by U.S. integrated steel producers, meaning that iron 
  1765  foundries (like electric arc furnace steel producers) are reliant on 
  1766  imported pig iron. Commenters also noted that other third-country 
  1767  sources of pig iron were limited given that China consumes virtually 
  1768  all of the pig iron it produces, and supply from Russia and Ukraine has 
  1769  been affected by the Russia-Ukraine war. Commenters also stated that 
  1770  pig iron is an essential raw material for iron foundry operations, and 
  1771  that it is melted and mixed with scrap iron and other alloys to produce 
  1772  cast iron. The comments observed that there is no substitute for pig 
  1773  iron, and that additional tariffs on pig iron imports would exacerbate 
  1774  competition they already face from imports of downstream products.
  1775      With respect to certain ferrous products, including pellets, 
  1776  turnings, shavings, chips, fillings, trimmings, and stampings, 
  1777  commenters noted that these products are similar to other products that 
  1778  were proposed to be exempted from tariffs applied pursuant to this 
  1779  action. The comments noted that, like other products already proposed 
  1780  for exemption, iron and steel waste and scrap are important inputs for 
  1781  carbon and alloy steel production, and there is no viable domestic 
  1782  supply for these products.
  1783      With respect to aluminum scrap and waste, commenters noted it is 
  1784  key feedstock material for the U.S. aluminum industry and imposing 
  1785  tariffs would disrupt the supply chains, negatively impacting U.S. 
  1786  aluminum production and, in turn, harming downstream industries and the 
  1787  U.S. economy.
  1788      With respect to aluminum hydroxide, commenters noted that the sole 
  1789  U.S. supplier of aluminum hydroxide is unable to meet U.S. demand and 
  1790  that approximately 40 percent of U.S. supply is sourced from Brazil, 
  1791  with remaining supply supported by producers in Germany and 
  1792  T[uuml]rkiye, among others. According to comments, aluminum hydroxide 
  1793  is an essential, non-substitutable raw material used in critical 
  1794  applications such as sanitation of drinking water, production of flame-
  1795  retardant polymer materials used in defense and industrial 
  1796  applications, production of oil and gas, and refining of aluminum. 
  1797  Companies that use aluminum hydroxide in these and other applications 
  1798  require a stable and cost-effective supply of aluminum hydroxide.
  1799      With respect to ash containing precious metals or precious metal 
  1800  compounds, commenters noted that tariffs on these items would increase 
  1801  costs and disrupt supply chains for products needed to protect U.S. 
  1802  national security, U.S. critical mineral security, and medical device 
  1803  supply chains.
  1804      With respect to certain battery waste and scrap, commenters noted 
  1805  that these products, which are crucial inputs for, among other things, 
  1806  communications and safety technologies, are not available from U.S. 
  1807  manufacturers in sufficient quantities or at commercially reasonable

summary.text: Verifying tariff exemption claims by cross-referencing net MFN economies and annex parts for Japan and Korea.Checking additional product counts and duty-cap rules against FTZ and severability clauses.Cataloging discrepancies between recital language and operative clauses across proclamations and notices.Identifying additional discrepancies in effective dates, scope language, and exemption listings across notices and annexes.Flagging new inconsistencies in enforcement language and nonexistent proclamation references.Consolidating Q3–Q5 and Q10 tariff scenarios with import, entry, and FTZ timing rules.Extending the tariff timeline to include Q5 product effective dates and Q10 duty stacking with exemption checks.Resolving USMCA exemption uncertainty for §338 and applying termination dates to IEEPA and §122 surcharges.Calculating §232 duty floors and USMCA carveouts across scenarios with termination dates.

Q11.answer:
1. §338 start date: Original operative text says Aug. 19 — Proc. 11046 para.9, clause (1), clause (3), 91 FR 46640-46641; same in 11047/11048. Later recitals repeat Aug. 19 — e.g. Proc. 11061 para.1, 91 FR 58311; Proc. 11064 para.1, 91 FR 58331. But 11061 para.4, 91 FR 58311, and every later recital para.4, say duties became effective Aug. 22 at 12:01 a.m. Operative suspension clause (1) makes Aug. 22 the effective date.
2. Suspension described as 3 days vs. date change: Proc. 11056 paras.4-5, 91 FR 54790, say suspending for a period of 3 days; operative clause (1), 91 FR 54790, does not impose a 3-day suspension that then expires by its own terms — it deletes Aug. 19 and inserts Aug. 22 in the Annex II chapeaus, and later documents treat Aug. 22 as the (indefinite) commencement date. Clause (2) also directs suspending collection, although on Aug. 18 collection had not yet begun under the Aug. 19 date.
3. Dairy scope proclamation that does not exist: Proc. 11062 clause (3), 91 FR 58320, says the exclusion does not otherwise affect products as established in the Sept. 8, 2026 dairy scope-modification proclamation. No dairy scope proclamation was published in the series (only alcohol 11064 and motor 11065, 91 FR 58331, 58339). Alcohol/motor exclusions correctly cite their scope proclamations.
4. §301 proposal category misdescribed: Memo recital, 91 FR 47719, describes the proposed 10% group as economies that impose a ban but do not yet effectively enforce it (Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan). June proposal §III-IV, 91 FR 34274, lists those six as having failed to effectively enforce (not failed to impose) and proposes 10% for economies that impose a ban. USTR notice summary, 91 FR 47318, likewise says proposed 10% was for economies that impose a ban/ART/partial regime, omitting the memo's formulation.
5. All-failed-both vs. lists: USTR notice §I, 91 FR 47318, lists 54 economies that failed to impose and effectively enforce and six that failed to effectively enforce, then states all have failed to impose and to effectively enforce (failed both). June proposal, 91 FR 34274, contains the same concluding sentence. The six-economy list is inconsistent with the all-failed-both conclusion.
6. Textile mechanism rate in proposal: Memo recital, 91 FR 47719, says USTR proposed a textile mechanism allowing imports at a zero §301 rate. June proposal §IV, 91 FR 34274, says the proposal would allow textile/apparel imports at a reduced §301 rate (volume tied to U.S. textile/cotton exports). Adopted TRQs are free of §301 duty, Memo §2, 91 FR 47721.
7. §301 summary conflates net-rate economies: USTR notice SUMMARY, 91 FR 47318, describes 10% for ban/ART/partial economies with specific economies at 10% net, implying net treatment is within the 10% group. Operative Memo §1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720, and §II.B, 91 FR 47323-47327, impose 12.5% net for Japan, Korea and Switzerland — outside the 10% group.
8. TRQ timing: Memo recital, 91 FR 47720, says TRQs will be feasible by Sept. 1, 2026. Operative Memo §2(a),(b), 91 FR 47721, directs establishment as soon as USTR determines it is feasible, with no Sept. 1 deadline.
9. §301 FTZ wording vs. §338 FTZ wording is not a discrepancy in rate, but in USTR notice §II.A, 91 FR 47321, FTZ privileged-foreign-status is effective as of the date the duty is imposed, whereas §338 original clause (4), 91 FR 46641, applies to FTZ admissions on/after the effective date; the §301 DATES line, 91 FR 47318, gives July 24 while Annex I.B, 91 FR 47394, later (July 31) adds the patented-pharmaceutical exemption without the DATES line disclosing it. These are noted as descriptive gaps, not operative conflicts, and are listed once here.
10. Scope-proclamation waiting period: Scope recitals, e.g. Proc. 11064 para.8, 91 FR 58332; Proc. 11076 para.9, 91 FR 68862, recite §338 duties may not take effect earlier than 30 days after the finding proclamation, yet operative scope clauses apply 7 days after signing (Sept. 8→Sept. 15; Oct. 23→Oct. 30). The scope documents do not explain the fit; they rely on the same paragraph's authority to suspend/revoke/supplement/amend.
Q11.basis: Citations in each numbered item above, with operative clauses distinguished from recitals/preamble. Drafting checked against Memo §§1-2, 91 FR 47720-47721; USTR notice §§I-II, 91 FR 47318-47321; June proposal §§III-IV, 91 FR 34274; §338 procs. 11046-11076 as cited.

Q11.answer:
1. §338 start date: Original operative text says Aug. 19 — Proc. 11046 para.9, clause (1), clause (3), 91 FR 46640-46641; same in 11047/11048. Later recitals repeat Aug. 19 — e.g. Proc. 11061 para.1, 91 FR 58311; Proc. 11064 para.1, 91 FR 58331. But 11061 para.4, 91 FR 58311, and every later recital para.4, say duties became effective Aug. 22 at 12:01 a.m. Operative suspension clause (1) makes Aug. 22 the effective date.
2. Suspension described as 3 days vs. date change: Proc. 11056 paras.4-5, 91 FR 54790, say suspending for a period of 3 days; operative clause (1), 91 FR 54790, does not impose a 3-day suspension that then expires by its own terms — it deletes Aug. 19 and inserts Aug. 22 in the Annex II chapeaus, and later documents treat Aug. 22 as the (indefinite) commencement date. Clause (2) also directs suspending collection, although on Aug. 18 collection had not yet begun under the Aug. 19 date.
3. Dairy scope proclamation that does not exist: Proc. 11062 clause (3), 91 FR 58320, says the exclusion does not otherwise affect products as established in the Sept. 8, 2026 dairy scope-modification proclamation. No dairy scope proclamation was published in the series (only alcohol 11064 and motor 11065, 91 FR 58331, 58339). Alcohol/motor exclusions correctly cite their scope proclamations.
4. §301 proposal category misdescribed: Memo recital, 91 FR 47719, describes the proposed 10% group as economies that impose a ban but do not yet effectively enforce it (Canada, Ecuador, EU, Indonesia, Mexico, Pakistan). June proposal §III-IV, 91 FR 34274, lists those six as having failed to effectively enforce (not failed to impose) and proposes 10% for economies that impose a ban. USTR notice summary, 91 FR 47318, likewise says proposed 10% was for economies that impose a ban/ART/partial regime, omitting the memo's formulation.
5. All-failed-both vs. lists: USTR notice §I, 91 FR 47318, lists 54 economies that failed to impose and effectively enforce and six that failed to effectively enforce, then states all have failed to impose and to effectively enforce (failed both). June proposal, 91 FR 34274, contains the same concluding sentence. The six-economy list is inconsistent with the all-failed-both conclusion.
6. Textile mechanism rate in proposal: Memo recital, 91 FR 47719, says USTR proposed a textile mechanism allowing imports at a zero §301 rate. June proposal §IV, 91 FR 34274, says the proposal would allow textile/apparel imports at a reduced §301 rate (volume tied to U.S. textile/cotton exports). Adopted TRQs are free of §301 duty, Memo §2, 91 FR 47721.
7. §301 summary conflates net-rate economies: USTR notice SUMMARY, 91 FR 47318, describes 10% for ban/ART/partial economies with specific economies at 10% net, implying net treatment is within the 10% group. Operative Memo §1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720, and §II.B, 91 FR 47323-47327, impose 12.5% net for Japan, Korea and Switzerland — outside the 10% group.
8. TRQ timing: Memo recital, 91 FR 47720, says TRQs will be feasible by Sept. 1, 2026. Operative Memo §2(a),(b), 91 FR 47721, directs establishment as soon as USTR determines it is feasible, with no Sept. 1 deadline.
9. §301 FTZ wording vs. §338 FTZ wording is not a discrepancy in rate, but in USTR notice §II.A, 91 FR 47321, FTZ privileged-foreign-status is effective as of the date the duty is imposed, whereas §338 original clause (4), 91 FR 46641, applies to FTZ admissions on/after the effective date; the §301 DATES line, 91 FR 47318, gives July 24 while Annex I.B, 91 FR 47394, later (July 31) adds the patented-pharmaceutical exemption without the DATES line disclosing it. These are noted as descriptive gaps, not operative conflicts, and are listed once here.
10. Scope-proclamation waiting period: Scope recitals, e.g. Proc. 11064 para.8, 91 FR 58332; Proc. 11076 para.9, 91 FR 68862, recite §338 duties may not take effect earlier than 30 days after the finding proclamation, yet operative scope clauses apply 7 days after signing (Sept. 8→Sept. 15; Oct. 23→Oct. 30). The scope documents do not explain the fit; they rely on the same paragraph's authority to suspend/revoke/supplement/amend.

Q14.answer:
1. Partly correct. Memo recital, 91 FR 47720, says TRQs are not feasible now but will be feasible by Sept. 1, 2026. Operative §2, 91 FR 47721, says as soon as USTR determines it is feasible — no Sept. 1 deadline.
2. Incorrect for the June proposal. Over 450 comments/nearly 60 witnesses describes the March initiation round, June proposal §I, 91 FR 34273. For the June proposal, USTR received over 1,600 written comments and over 100 witnesses, Memo, 91 FR 47719; USTR notice §I, 91 FR 47319.
3. Partly correct. Seven economies moved to 10%: six adopted bans (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago) and Jordan undertook an ART commitment, Memo, 91 FR 47720; USTR notice §I, 91 FR 47319. Not each adopted a ban.
4. Incorrect. Commenters suggested removing beef/avocados (and paprika, lithium hexafluorophosphate, forgings) linking them to forced labor, USTR notice §III.C.3, 91 FR 47331. USTR determined not to remove these products.

EU (Part C), Taiwan (Part K) and Switzerland (Part D) have economy-specific Annex II parts, but Japan and Korea are excepted only by Annex I and Annex II Part A, §§II.B.28, 49, 91 FR 47324, 47327 — no own negotiated list.
6. Partly correct. USTR excluded an additional 471 products in each investigation, §III.D, 91 FR 47331, and exempted certain sugar and sugar-containing products, §§III.D, 91 FR 47331-47333 — not all sugar products.
7. Incorrect. Only net-rate economies are capped so MFN+§301 =10% or 12.5%, §§II.B.19, 28, 51, 52, 91 FR 47323-47327. Flat-rate economies pay §301 in addition to MFN, Note 52(a), 91 FR 47352 (e.g. MFN 4% +12.5% =16.5%).
8. Correct. USTR notice §II.A, 91 FR 47321: FTZ-admitted products subject to the duty, except domestic-status-eligible, only may be admitted as privileged foreign status, effective as of the date the duty is imposed.
9. Correct. Memo §4(e), 91 FR 47723; USTR notice §IV, 91 FR 47335: if an exemption is held invalid, the applicable tariff applies to imports to which the invalidated exemption applied before invalidation.
10. Correct. USTR notice §III.C, 91 FR 47330: exempt all Annex A proposed products except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals; determined not to remove additional products.
